e-599.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve Given the First Derivative
e-599.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x =e^{t}, \, y= e^{2t}+1.$ Given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= 2e^t,$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
e-599.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= 2e^t,$ and we can calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} (e^t) = e^t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(2{e}^{t})}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6803.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve
e-6803.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=e^t, y=2e^{2t}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
e-6803.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t, \qquad y'(t)=4e^{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4e^{2t}}{e^t} = 4e^t.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(4{e}^{t})}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

e-600.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
e-600.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x =  \sin(2t), \qquad y= 2\cos (2t) \qquad 0 \leq t \lt \pi.
$$

Given that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = -2 \tan(2t),$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}$ at the point where $t=\dfrac\pi 8.$
e-600.worked_solution:
To compute $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y }{\textrm d x^2},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= -2 \tan(2t),$ and we can calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} ( \sin 2t ) = 2 \cos(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-2\operatorname{tan}⁡2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}{|}_{t=\pi /8} & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-2{(\sqrt{2})}^{3} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t2−1,y=e−4t. Given that dydx=−2e−4tt, calculate d2ydx2.

a
2e−4t(t+1)t2
b
e−2t(4t+1)t2
c
e−4t(4t+1)t3
d
e−4t(2t−1)t3
e
e−4t(1−2t)t3
Submit

decision.explanation: Use d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt). Differentiating -2e^(-4t)/t gives 8e^(-4t)/t + 2e^(-4t)/t². Dividing by dx/dt = 2t gives e^(-4t)(4t+1)/t³.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{2}-1,\,y={e}^{-4t}.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2}-1)=2t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{{t}^{2}})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{2{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4t}(4t+1)}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t2−1,y=e−4t. Given that dydx=−2e−4tt, calculate d2ydx2.

a
2e−4t(t+1)t2
b
e−2t(4t+1)t2
c
e−4t(4t+1)t3
d
e−4t(2t−1)t3

Submit

EXPLANATION

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

d2ydx2=ddt(dydx)(dxdt).

We're given that dydx=−2e−4tt, and we can calculate dxdt as follows:

dxdt=ddt(t2−1)=2t

Substituting into the formula, we get

d2ydx2=ddt(−2e−4tt)2t=(8te−4t+2e−4tt2)2t=8te−4t+2e−4t2t3=e−4t(4t+1)t3.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve Given the First Derivative
content.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{2}-1,\,y={e}^{-4t}.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2}-1)=2t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{-2{e}^{-4t}}{t})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{{t}^{2}})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{8t{e}^{-4t}+2{e}^{-4t}}{2{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4t}(4t+1)}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={e}^{2t},\,y={e}^{4t}.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2{e}^{2t},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2{e}^{2t},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({e}^{2t})=2{e}^{2t}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(2{e}^{2t})}{2{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2t}}{2{e}^{2t}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=3\operatorname{cot}⁡t,$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(3\operatorname{cot}⁡t)}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{-3{csc}^{2}⁡t}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =3{csc}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-3.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t))}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}=-\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}

$$

after.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{3}+6,\,y=3{t}^{6}-3$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=18{t}^{5}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{18{t}^{5}}{3{t}^{2}}=6{t}^{3}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(6{t}^{3})}{3{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{18{t}^{2}}{3{t}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

dydx=y′(t)x′(t).

Differentiating x and y, we get

x′(t)=6e3t,y′(t)=3et+2.

Therefore, dydx=3et+26e3t=12e2−2t.

d2ydx2=ddt(dydx)(dxdt).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve
content.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=2{e}^{3t},\,y=3{e}^{t+2}-5$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6{e}^{3t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{e}^{t+2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3{e}^{t+2}}{6{e}^{3t}}=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2-2t}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2-2t})}{6{e}^{3t}} \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{2-2t}}{6{e}^{3t}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}{e}^{2-5t}.\end{aligned}
$$

dydx=y′(t)x′(t).

Differentiating x and y, we get

x′(t)=t2,y′(t)=5t4+6t2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve
content.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\frac{{t}^{3}}{3},\,y={t}^{5}+2{t}^{3}$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}+6{t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5{t}^{4}+6{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}=5{t}^{2}+6.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(5{t}^{2}+6)}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}{5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)}=-2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5t).

dydx=y′(t)x′(t).

content.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)-4,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+7.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}{5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)}=-2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-2\operatorname{tan}⁡(5t))}{5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)} \\  & =-\frac{10{sec}^{2}⁡(5t)}{5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)} \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(5t).\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: A curve has parametric equations $x=\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-2,\,y={t}^{7}+2.$ Given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=7{t}^{2},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ at the point where $t=2.$
after.worked_solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=7{t}^{2},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-2)={t}^{4}.
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(7{t}^{2})}{{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{14t}{{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{14}{{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=2,$ and we get

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{t=2}=\frac{14}{(2)^{3}}=\frac{14}{8}=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=5t,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{4}-5)=4{t}^{3}.

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(5t)}{4{t}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4{t}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=1,$ and we get

$$
{\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}|}_{t=1}=\frac{5}{4(1)^{3}}=\frac{5}{4}.
$$
